{{Short description|Critical point where a periodic solution arises}}
[[File:Hopfeigenvalues.png|thumb|Complex eigenvalues of a fixed point of an arbitrary differential equation (dots). In case of the Hopf bifurcation, two distinct complex conjugate eigenvalues cross the imaginary axis.]]
In the [[mathematics]] of [[dynamical system]]s and [[differential equation]]s, a '''Hopf bifurcation''' is said to occur when varying a parameter of the system causes the set of solutions (trajectories) to change from being attracted to (or repelled by) a [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]], and instead become attracted to (or repelled by) an [[periodic function|oscillatory, periodic solution]].<ref>{{Cite web|url =https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/mathematics/18-385j-nonlinear-dynamics-and-chaos-fall-2004/lecture-notes/hopfbif.pdf |title = Hopf Bifurcations.|publisher = MIT}}</ref> The Hopf bifurcation is a two-dimensional analog of the [[pitchfork bifurcation]].

Many different kinds of systems exhibit Hopf bifurcations, from [[van der Pol oscillator|radio oscillators]] to [[Bogie|railroad bogies]].<ref name="Reza Serajian"/> [[Trailer (vehicle)|Trailers]] towed behind [[automobile]]s become infamously unstable if loaded incorrectly, or if designed with the wrong geometry. This offers an intuitive example of a Hopf bifurcation in the ordinary world, where stable motion becomes unstable and oscillatory as a parameter is varied. Fluid flows also exhibit Hopf bifurcation behavior when the transition from steady to unsteady [[laminar flow]] occurs.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Agnaou
 |first1=M.
 |last2=Lasseux
 |first2=D.
 |last3=Ahmadi
 |first3=A.
 |title=From steady to unsteady laminar flow in model porous structures: an investigation of the first Hopf bifurcation
 |journal=[[Computers & Fluids]]
 |volume=136
 |pages=67–82
 |year=2016
 |issn=0045-7930
 |doi=10.1016/j.compfluid.2016.05.030
 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045793016301797
|hdl=10985/10895
 |hdl-access=free
 }}</ref>

The general theory of how the solution sets of dynamical systems change in response to changes of parameters is called [[bifurcation theory]]; the term ''bifurcation'' arises, as the set of solutions typically split into several classes. [[Stability theory]] pursues the general theory of stability in mechanical, electronic and biological systems.

The conventional approach to locating Hopf bifurcations is to work with the [[Jacobian matrix]] associated with the system of differential equations. When this matrix has a pair of complex-conjugate [[eigenvalue]]s that cross the imaginary axis as a parameter is varied, that point is the bifurcation. That crossing is associated with a stable fixed point "bifurcating" into a [[limit cycle]].

A Hopf bifurcation is also known as a '''Poincaré&ndash;Andronov&ndash;Hopf bifurcation''', named after [[Henri Poincaré]], [[Aleksandr Andronov]] and [[Eberhard Hopf]].

== Overview ==

=== Normal form ===
Hopf bifurcations occur in a large variety of dynamical systems described by differential equations. Near such a bifurcation, a two-dimensional subset  of the dynamical system is approximated by a [[normal form (bifurcation theory)|normal form]], canonically expressed as the following time-dependent differential equation:

<math display="block">\frac{dz}{dt}=z\left((\lambda + i ) + b |z|^2\right)</math>

Here <math>z</math> is the dynamical variable; it is a [[complex number]]. The parameter <math>\lambda</math> is real, and <math>b=\alpha + i \beta</math> is a complex parameter. The number <math>\alpha</math> is called the '''[[Lyapunov equation|first Lyapunov coefficient]]'''. The above has a simple exact solution, given below. This solution exhibits two distinct behaviors, depending on whether <math>\lambda >0</math> or <math>\lambda <0</math>. This change of behavior, as a function of <math>\lambda ,</math> is termed the "Hopf bifurcation".

The study of Hopf bifurcations is not so much the study of the above and its solution, as it is the study of how such two-dimensional subspaces can be identified and mapped onto this normal form. One approach is to examine the [[eigenvalue]]s of the [[Jacobian matrix]] of the differential equations as a parameter is varied near the bifurcation point.

=== Simplified normal form ===
For example, if we analyze the following system of two ordinary differential equations depending on one parameter <math>\alpha    
</math>,<math display="block">\begin{cases}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}x_1}{\mathrm{dt}} = \alpha x_1 - x_2 - x_1(x_1^2 + x_2^2) \\
    \frac{\mathrm{d}x_2}{\mathrm{dt}} = x_1 + \alpha x_2 - x_2(x_1^2 + x_2^2)
\end{cases}\ ,</math>and examine the Jacobian matrix <math>J
</math> of the equilibrium solution <math>(x_1, x_2) = (0,0)
</math>, we find that it is of the form<math display="block">J = \begin{pmatrix}
    \alpha & -1 \\
    1 & \alpha
\end{pmatrix},
</math>with eigenvalues <math>\lambda_{1;2} = \alpha \pm \mathrm{i}
</math> (where <math>\mathrm i
</math> is the imaginary unit). This allows us to rewrite the system by introducing a new complex variable <math>z = x_1 + \mathrm{i} x_2
</math> such that <math>\overline z = x_1 - \mathrm{i} x_2
</math>, and consequently, <math>|\overline z|^2 = z \overline z = x_1^2 + x_2^2
</math>. Due to the linearity of differentiation,<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{\mathrm{d}x_1}{\mathrm{dt}} + \mathrm{i}\frac{\mathrm{d}x_2}{\mathrm{dt}} = \alpha(x_1 + \mathrm{i} x_2) + \mathrm{i}(x_1 + \mathrm{i}x_2) - (x_1 + \mathrm{i}x_2)(x_1^2 + x_2^2) = (\alpha + \mathrm{i})z - z|z|^2,
</math>which is the desired normal form, with parameters <math>\lambda = \alpha 
</math> and <math>b=-z 
</math>.<ref name=":1">{{Citation |last=Kuznetsov |first=Yuri A. |chapter=One-Parameter Bifurcations of Equilibria in Continuous-Time Dynamical Systems |date=2023 |title=Elements of Applied Bifurcation Theory |pages=89–128 |editor-last=Kuznetsov |editor-first=Yuri A. |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-22007-4_3 |isbn=978-3-031-22007-4}}</ref>

==== Representation in polar coordinates ====
Since the example above is expressed in terms of complex variables, we can easily convert it to a two-variable system of ordinary differential equations using polar coordinates.<ref name=":1" /> Setting <math>z = r \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}</math> (see {{Section link|Complex number|Polar form}}), we obtain<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{dt}} \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi} + r\mathrm{i}\frac{\mathrm{d}\varphi}{\mathrm{dt}}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi} = r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}(\alpha + \mathrm{i} - r^2). 
</math>Dividing by <math>\mathrm{e}^{i\varphi}
</math> and simplifying yields the equation <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{dt}} + \mathrm{i} r \frac{\mathrm{d}\varphi}{\mathrm{dt}} = r(\alpha - r^2) + \mathrm{i}r 
</math>. Since both <math>r 
</math> and <math>\varphi 
</math> are real variables, the real and imaginary components can be separated, and we get the resulting polar form of the system:<math display="block">\begin{cases}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{dt}} = r(\alpha - r^2) \\
    \frac{\mathrm{d}\varphi}{\mathrm{dt}} = 1
\end{cases}</math>Alternatively, we could have derived the same polar representation directly by setting <math>x_1 = r \cos (\varphi)
</math> and <math>x_2 = r \sin(\varphi)
</math>.

=== Exact solution ===
[[Image:Supercritical Hopf bifurcation.gif|thumb|right|Visualization of the normal form of the supercritical Hopf bifurcation.<ref>Heitmann, S., Breakspear, M (2017-2022) Brain Dynamics Toolbox. [https://bdtoolbox.org bdtoolbox.org] [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5625923 doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5625923]</ref>]]

The normal form is effectively the [[Stuart–Landau equation]], written with a different parametrization. It has a simple exact solution in polar coordinates. Writing <math>z=re^{i\theta}</math> and considering the real and imaginary parts as distinct, one obtains a pair of ordinary differential equations:
<math display="block">\frac{d\theta}{dt} = 1+\beta r^2</math>
and
<math display="block">\frac{dr}{dt} = r\left(\lambda +\alpha r^2\right).</math>
The second equation can be solved by observing that it is linear in <math>1/r^2</math>. That is,
<math display="block">\frac {d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{r^2}\right) = -2\left(\frac{\lambda}{r^2}+\alpha\right)</math>
which is just the shifted [[exponential equation]]. Re-arranging gives the generic solution 
<math display="block">r(t)=r_0\sqrt \frac{\lambda}{\left(\lambda +\alpha r_0^2\right)e^{-2\lambda t}-\alpha r_0^2}</math>

Depending on the sign of <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\alpha</math>, the trajectory of a point can be seen to spiral in to the origin, spiral out to infinity, or to approach a [[limit cycle]].

=== Supercritical and subcritical Hopf bifurcations ===
[[File:Hopfbifurcation.png|thumb|400px|Dynamics of the Hopf bifurcation near <math>\lambda=0</math>. Possible trajectories in red, stable structures in dark blue and unstable structures in dashed light blue. Supercritical Hopf bifurcation: 1a) stable fixed point 1b) unstable fixed point, stable limit cycle 1c) phase space dynamics. Subcritical Hopf bifurcation: 2a) stable fixed point, unstable limit cycle 2b) unstable fixed point 2c) phase space dynamics. <math>\omega</math> determines the angular dynamics and therefore the direction of winding for the trajectories.]]

The limit cycle is orbitally stable if the first Lyapunov coefficient <math>\alpha</math> is negative, and if <math>\lambda > 0.</math> Then the bifurcation is said to be '''supercritical'''. Otherwise it is unstable and the bifurcation is '''subcritical'''.

If <math>\alpha</math> is negative then there is a stable limit cycle for <math>\lambda >0 :</math>
<math display="block"> z(t) = r e^{i \omega t}</math>
where
<math display="block"> r=\sqrt{-\lambda/\alpha}\quad\text{ and }\quad\omega= 1 + \beta r^2.</math>
This is the supercritical regime.

If <math>\alpha</math> is positive then there is an unstable limit cycle for <math>\lambda <0 .</math>  The bifurcation is said to be subcritical. This classification into sub and super-critical bifurcations is analogous to that of the [[pitchfork bifurcation]].

=== Jacobian ===
The Hopf bifurcation can be understood by examining the [[eigenvalue]]s of the [[Jacobian matrix]] for the normal form. This is most readily done by re-writing the normal form in Cartesian coordinates <math>z=x+iy</math>. It then has the form
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot{x}	&=\lambda x-y+\left(\alpha x-\beta y\right)\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right) \\
\dot{y}	&=x+\lambda y+\left(\beta x+\alpha y\right)\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right) \\
\end{align}</math>
where the shorthand <math>\dot{x} = dx/dt</math> and <math>\dot{y} = dy/dt</math> is used. The Jacobian is
<math display="block">J=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{\partial\dot{x}}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial\dot{x}}{\partial y}\\
\frac{\partial\dot{y}}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial\dot{y}}{\partial y}
\end{array}\right]
</math>
This is a bit tedious to compute:
<math display="block">
J=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\lambda+3\alpha x^{2}-2\beta xy+\alpha y^{2}\quad & -1-3\beta y^{2}+2\alpha xy-\beta x^{2}\\
1+3\beta x^{2}+2\alpha xy+\beta y^{2}\quad & \lambda+3\alpha y^{2}+2\beta xy+\alpha x^{2}
\end{array}\right]
</math>
The fixed point was previously identified to be located at <math>x=y=0</math>, at which location the Jacobian takes the particularly simple form:
<math display="block">J=
\left[\begin{array}{cc}
\lambda & -1\\
1 & \lambda
\end{array}\right]
</math>
The corresponding [[characteristic polynomial]] is 
<math display="block">0 =\det [J-wI] = \left(\lambda-w\right)^2 +1 </math>
which has solutions
<math display="block">w=\lambda\pm i</math>
Here, <math>w</math> is a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues of the Jacobian. When the parameter <math>\lambda</math> is negative, the real part of the eigenvalues is (obviously) negative. As the parameter crosses zero, the real part vanishes: this is the Hopf bifurcation. As previously seen, the limit cycle arises as <math>\lambda</math> goes positive if <math> \alpha<0 </math>.

All Hopf bifurcations have this general form: the Jacobian matrix has a pair of complex-conjugate eigenvalues that cross the imaginary axis as the pertinent parameter is varied.

=== Linearization ===
The above computation of the Jacobian can be significantly simplified by working in the [[tangent plane]], tangent to the fixed point. The fixed point is located at <math>(x,y)=(0,0)</math> and so one can "linearize" the differential equation by dropping all terms that are higher than linear order.  This gives

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot{x}	&=\lambda x-y \\
\dot{y}	&=x+\lambda y \\
\end{align}</math>

The Jacobian is computed exactly as before; nothing has changed, except to make the calculations simpler. The linearized differential equation can be recognized as being given by a [[Lie derivative]] defined on the [[tangent bundle]]. Because all cotangent bundles are always [[symplectic manifold]]s, it is common to formulate bifurcation theory in terms of [[symplectic geometry]].<ref name="Marsden">Abraham, R.; Marsden, J. E. (2008). Foundations of Mechanics: A Mathematical Exposition of Classical Mechanics with an Introduction to the Qualitative Theory of Dynamical Systems (2nd ed.). AMS Chelsea Publishing. ISBN 978-0-8218-4438-0.</ref>

=== Examples ===
[[Image:hopf-bif.gif|thumb|250px|right|The Hopf bifurcation in the Selkov system (see article). As the parameters change, a [[limit cycle]] (in blue) appears out of a stable equilibrium.]]

Hopf bifurcations occur in the [[Lotka–Volterra equations|Lotka–Volterra model]] of [[Predation|predator–prey interaction]] (known as [[paradox of enrichment]]), the [[Hodgkin–Huxley model]] for nerve [[membrane potential]],<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Guckenheimer | first1 = J.
 | last2 = Labouriau | first2 = J.S.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02460693
 | issue = 5
 | journal = Bulletin of Mathematical Biology
 | pages = 937–952
 | title = Bifurcation of the Hodgkin and Huxley equations: A new twist
 | volume = 55
 | year = 1993| s2cid = 189888352
 }}.</ref> the Selkov model of [[glycolysis]],<ref name="Selkov Model">{{cite web| title=Selkov Model Wolfram Demo| work=[demonstrations.wolfram.com ]|url=http://demonstrations.wolfram.com/HopfBifurcationInTheSelkovModel/|access-date=30 September 2012}}</ref> the [[Belousov&ndash;Zhabotinsky reaction]], the [[Lorenz attractor]], the [[Brusselator]], the [[delay differential equation]] and in [[classical electromagnetism]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=López|first=Álvaro G|date=2020-12-01|title=Stability analysis of the uniform motion of electrodynamic bodies|journal=Physica Scripta|language=en|volume=96|issue=1|page=015506|doi=10.1088/1402-4896/abcad2|s2cid=228919333 |issn=1402-4896}}</ref> Hopf bifurcations have also been shown to occur in fission waves.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Osborne |first1=Andrew G. |last2=Deinert |first2=Mark R. |date=October 2021 |title=Stability instability and Hopf bifurcation in fission waves |journal=Cell Reports Physical Science |language=en |volume=2 |issue=10 |article-number=100588 |doi=10.1016/j.xcrp.2021.100588|bibcode=2021CRPS....200588O |s2cid=240589650 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The Selkov model is

<math display="block"> \frac{dx}{dt} = -x + ay + x^2 y, ~~ \frac{dy}{dt} = b - a y - x^2 y. </math>

The figure shows a [[phase portrait]] illustrating the Hopf bifurcation in the Selkov model.<ref name="Strogatz1994">For detailed derivation, see {{cite book |title= Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos |last= Strogatz |first= Steven H. |year= 1994 |publisher= Addison Wesley |isbn= 978-0-7382-0453-6 |page= [https://archive.org/details/nonlineardynamic00stro/page/205 205] |url-access= registration |url= https://archive.org/details/nonlineardynamic00stro/page/205 }}</ref>

In railway vehicle systems, Hopf bifurcation analysis is notably important. Conventionally a railway vehicle's stable motion at low speeds crosses over to unstable at high speeds. One aim of the nonlinear analysis of these systems is to perform an analytical investigation of bifurcation, nonlinear lateral stability and hunting behavior of rail vehicles on a tangent track, which uses the [[Bogoliubov method]].<ref name="Reza Serajian">{{cite journal|last1=Serajian |first1=Reza |year=2011 |title=Effects of the bogie and body inertia on the nonlinear wheel-set hunting recognized by the hopf bifurcation theory |url=http://www.iust.ac.ir/ijae/article-1-25-en.pdf |journal=International Journal of Automotive Engineering |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=186&ndash;196}}</ref>

=== Geometric interpretation ===
The benefit of the abstract formulation in terms of [[symplectic geometry]] is that it enables a geometric intuition into what otherwise seem to be complicated dynamical systems.

Consider the space of all possible solutions (point trajectories) to some set of differential equations. The tangent vectors to these solutions lie in the [[phase space]] for that system; more formally, in the tangent bundle. The phase space can be divided into three parts: the [[stable manifold]], the [[unstable manifold]], and the [[center manifold]]. The stable manifold consists of all of the tangent vector fields that, upon integration, approach the limit point or limit cycle. The unstable manifold consist of those vector fields that point away from the limit-point/limit cycle. The center manifold consists of the points on the limit, together with their tangent vectors.

The Hopf bifurcation is a rearrangement of these manifolds, as parameters are varied. For the normal form, the phase space is four-dimensional: the two coordinates <math>x,y</math> and the two velocities <math>\dot{x},\dot{y}.</math> When <math>\lambda<0</math> (and <math>\alpha<0</math>) the entire (four-dimensional) space of solutions belongs to the stable manifold. As <math>\lambda</math> is varied, the center manifold changes from a point to a circle. As <math>\alpha</math> is varied, the stable manifold flips to become unstable.

In a general setting, the abstraction allows a four-dimensional subspace to be isolated from the full system, and then, as parameters are varied, all changes to the overall geometry are isolated to that four-dimensional subspace.

== Formal definition of a Hopf bifurcation ==

The appearance or the disappearance of a periodic orbit through a local change in the stability properties of a fixed point is known as the Hopf bifurcation. The following theorem works for fixed points with one pair of conjugate nonzero purely imaginary [[eigenvalue]]s. It tells the conditions under which this bifurcation phenomenon occurs.

'''Theorem''' (see section 11.2 of <ref name="HaleKocak1991"/>). Let <math>J</math> be the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] of a continuous parametric [[dynamical system]] evaluated at a fixed point. Suppose that all eigenvalues of <math>J</math> have negative real part except for one conjugate pair, varying as <math>\rho \pm i\epsilon</math> for some function <math>\rho</math> of the parameters. A '''Hopf bifurcation''' arises when this eigenvalue pair cross the imaginary axis. This occurs as <math>\rho</math> changes from negative to positive as the system parameters are varied.

== Routh&ndash;Hurwitz criterion ==
The [[Routh–Hurwitz stability criterion|Routh&ndash;Hurwitz criterion]] (section I.13 of <ref name="HairerNorsettWanner1993"/>) gives necessary conditions for a Hopf bifurcation to occur.<ref name="KahouiWeber2000"/>

=== Sturm series ===
Let <math>p_0,~p_1,~\dots~,~p_k</math> be [[Sturm series]] associated to a [[characteristic polynomial]] <math>P</math>. They can be written in the form:
<math display="block">
p_i(\mu)= c_{i,0} \mu^{k-i} + c_{i,1} \mu^{k-i-2} + c_{i,2} \mu^{k-i-4}+\cdots
</math>
The coefficients <math>c_{i,0}</math> for <math>i</math> in <math>\{1,~\dots~,~k\}</math> correspond to what is called [[Hurwitz determinants]].<ref name="KahouiWeber2000"/> Their definition is related to the associated [[Routh–Hurwitz matrix|Hurwitz matrix]].

=== Propositions ===
'''Proposition 1'''. If all the Hurwitz determinants <math>c_{i,0}</math> are positive, apart perhaps <math>c_{k,0}</math> then the associated Jacobian has no pure imaginary eigenvalues.

'''Proposition 2'''. If all Hurwitz determinants <math>c_{i,0}</math> (for all <math>i</math> in <math>\{0,~\dots~,~k-2\}</math> are positive, <math>c_{k-1,0}=0</math> and <math>c_{k-2,1}<0</math> then all the eigenvalues of the associated Jacobian have negative real parts except a purely imaginary conjugate pair.

The conditions that we are looking for so that a Hopf bifurcation occurs (see theorem above) for a parametric continuous dynamical system are given by this last proposition.

=== Example ===
Consider the classical [[Van der Pol oscillator]] written with ordinary differential equations:
<math display="block">
\left \{
\begin{array}{l}
\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \mu (1-y^2)x - y, \\
\dfrac{dy}{dt} = x.
\end{array}
\right .
</math>

The Jacobian matrix associated to this system is
<math display="block">
J = 
\begin{bmatrix}
-\mu (-1+y^2) & -2 \mu y x -1 \\
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
</math>

The characteristic polynomial (in <math>\lambda</math>) of the Jacobian at the fixed point <math>(x,y)=(0,0)</math> is
<math display="block">
P(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - \mu \lambda + 1.
</math>
The associated [[Sturm series]] is
<math display="block">
\begin{array}{l}
p_0(\lambda)=a_0 \lambda^2 -a_2 \\
p_1(\lambda)=a_1 \lambda
\end{array}
</math>
with coefficients <math>a_0=1, a_1=-\mu, a_2=1.</math>

The [[Sturm's theorem|Sturm polynomials]] can be written as (here <math>i=0,1</math>):
<math display="block">
p_i(\mu)= c_{i,0} \mu^{k-i} + c_{i,1} \mu^{k-i-2} + c_{i,2} \mu^{k-i-4}+\cdots
</math>
For the Van der Pol oscillator, the coefficients are
<math display="block">
c_{0,0} = 1,\qquad c_{1,0}=- \mu, \qquad c_{0,1}=-1. 
</math>

A Hopf bifurcation can occur when proposition 2 is satisfied; in the present case, proposition 2 requires that 
<math display="block">
c_{0,0} >0,\qquad c_{1,0}= 0, \qquad c_{0,1} <0. 
</math>

Clearly, the first and third conditions are satisfied; the second condition states that a Hopf bifurcation occurs for the Van der Pol oscillator when <math>\mu = 0</math>.

== Serial expansion method ==
The serial expansion method provides a way for obtaining explicit solutions containing a Hopf bifurcation by means of a [[perturbative expansion]] in the order parameter.<ref name=":0">[https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-385j-nonlinear-dynamics-and-chaos-fall-2014/c6f658c96c4ab007838a3dba51899a73_MIT18_385JF14_Hopf-Bif.pdf 18.385J / 2.036J Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos Fall 2014: Hopf Bifurcations]. MIT OpenCourseWare</ref>

Consider a system defined by <math>\ddot x + h(\dot x, x, \mu) = 0</math>, where <math>h</math> is smooth and <math>\mu</math> is a parameter. The parameter should be written so that as <math>\mu</math> increases from below zero to above zero, the origin turns from a spiral sink to a spiral source. A linear transform of parameters may be needed to place the equation into this form. For <math>\mu > 0</math>, a perturbative expansion is performed using [[two-timing]]:

<math display="block">x(t) = \epsilon x_1(t, T) + \epsilon^2 x_2(t, T) + \epsilon^3 x_3(t, T) + \cdots</math>

where <math>T = \nu t</math> is "slow-time" (thus "two-timing"), and <math>\epsilon, \nu</math> are functions of <math>\mu</math>. By an argument of [[harmonic balance]] (see <ref name=":0" /> for details), one may use <math>\epsilon = \mu^{1/2}, \nu = \mu</math>. Placing the perturbative expansion for <math>x(t)</math> into <math>\ddot x + h(\dot x, x, \mu) = 0</math>, and keeping terms up to the <math>\epsilon^3</math> produces three ordinary differential equations in <math>x_1, x_2, x_3</math>.

The first equation is of form <math>\partial_{tt} x_1 + \omega_0^2 x_1 = 0</math>, which is solved by <math>x_1(t, T) = A(T) \cos(\omega_0 t + \phi(T)).</math> The <math>A(T), \phi(T)</math> are "slowly varying" functions of <math>T</math>. Inserting this into the second equation allows it to be solved for <math>x_2(t, T)</math>.

Then plugging the solutions for <math>x_1, x_2</math> into the third equation, an equation of form <math>\partial_{tt} x_3 + \omega_0^2 x_3 = \cdots</math> is obtained, with the right-hand-side a sum of trigonometric terms. Of these terms, the "resonance term", the one containing <math>\cos(\omega_0 t), \sin(\omega_0 t)</math> must be set to zero. This is the same idea as in the [[Poincaré–Lindstedt method]]. This provides two ordinary differential equations for <math>A, \phi</math>, allowing one to solve for the equilibrium value of <math>A</math>, as well as its stability.

=== Example of serial expansion ===
Consider the system defined by 
<math display="block">\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\dot{x} &= \mu x+y-x^2 \\
\dot{y} &= -x+\mu y+2 x^2 \\
\end{array} \right .</math>

This system has an equilibrium point at origin. When <math>\mu</math> increases from negative to positive, the origin turns from a stable spiral point to an unstable spiral point. Eliminating <math>y</math> from the equations gives a single second-order differential equation
<math display="block">\ddot x - 2\mu \dot x + (1+\mu^2)x + 2x\dot x - (2 + \mu )x^2 = 0.</math>

The perturbative expansion to be performed is
<math display="block">x(t) = \epsilon x_1(t, T) + \epsilon^2 x_2(t, T) + \cdots</math>
with 
<math display="block">\epsilon = \mu^{1/2}, \qquad T = \mu t.</math> 
Expanding up to order <math>\epsilon^3</math> results in
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\partial_{tt}x_1 + x_1 = 0\\
\partial_{tt}x_2+ x_2 = 2x_1^2 - 2x_1 \partial_t x_1\\
\partial_{tt}x_3 + x_3 = 4x_1x_2 + 2\partial_t(x_1-x_1x_2 - \partial_T x_1)
\end{cases}</math>

The first equation has the solution 
<math display="block">x_1(t, T) = A(T) \cos(t + \phi(T)).</math>
Here <math>A(T), \phi(T)</math> are respectively the "slow-varying amplitude" and "slow-varying phase" of the simple oscillation. The second equation has solution
<math display="block">x_2(t, T) = B \cos(t + \theta) + A^2 - \frac 13 A^2(\sin(2t+2\phi) + \cos(2t+2\phi)),</math>
where <math>B, \theta</math> are also slow-varying amplitude and phase. The <math>B</math> and <math>\theta</math> terms can be absorbed into <math>A</math> and <math>\phi ;</math> equivalently, <math>B=0</math> can be set [[without loss of generality]]. To demonstrate this, the perturbative expansion is written as

<math display="block">\begin{align}
x &= \epsilon x_1 + \epsilon^2 x_2 + \cdots \\ 
  &= \epsilon(A \cos(t + \phi) + \epsilon B\cos(t+\theta)) + \cdots \\
\end{align}</math>

Basic [[trigonometry]] allows the two cosines to be merged into one:
<math display="block">A \cos(t + \phi) + \epsilon B\cos(t+\theta) = C \cos(t + \xi)</math>

for some <math>C</math> and <math>\xi.</math> But this has exactly the same form as <math>x_1.</math> Thus, the <math>B</math> term can be eliminated by redefining <math>A</math> to be <math>C</math> and <math>\xi</math> to be <math>\phi .</math> The solution to the second equation is thus

<math display="block">x_2(t, T) = A^2 - \frac 13 A^2(\sin(2t+2\phi) + \cos(2t+2\phi))</math>

Plugging through the third equation gives
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\partial_{tt} x_3 + x_3
  &= (2A-A^3-2A')\sin(t+\phi) \\
  &\quad - (2A\phi' +11A^3/3)\cos(t+\phi) \\
  &\quad + \frac 13 A^3(5\sin(3t+3\phi)-\cos(3t+3\phi))
\end{align}</math>

Eliminating the resonance term gives 
<math display="block">A' = A-A^3/2, \quad \phi' = -\frac{11}{6}A^2</math>

where the prime denotes differentiation by the slow time <math>T.</math> The first equation shows that <math>A= \sqrt 2</math> is a stable equilibrium. The Hopf bifurcation creates an attracting (rather than repelling) limit cycle.

Plugging in <math>A= \sqrt 2</math> gives <math>\phi = -\frac{11}{3}T + \phi_0</math>. The time coordinate can be shifted so that <math>\phi_0 = 0</math>. The third equation becomes

<math display="block">\partial_{tt} x_3 + x_3 = \frac 13 A^3(5\sin(3t+3\phi)-\cos(3t+3\phi))</math>

giving a solution

<math display="block">x_3 = \frac{\sqrt 2}{12}(5\sin(3t + 3\phi)-\cos(3t + 3\phi))</math>

Plugging in <math>A= \sqrt 2</math> back to the expressions for <math>x_1, x_2</math> gives

<math display="block">x_1 = \sqrt 2 \cos(t+\phi), \quad x_2 = 2-\frac 23 (\sin(2t+2\phi) + \cos(2t+2\phi))</math>

Plugging these back to <math>y = x^2 + \dot x - \mu x</math> yields the serial expansion of <math>y</math> as well, up to order <math>\mu^{3/2}</math>.

After writing <math>\theta := t + \phi</math> the solution is

<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
x &= \mu^{1/2} \sqrt{2} \cos\theta + \mu \left(-\frac 23 \sin(2\theta)-\frac 23 \cos(2\theta)+2\right) \\
  &\qquad + \mu^{3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{72}} \left( 5\sin(3\theta) - \cos(3\theta) \right) + \mathcal{O}(\mu^2)\\
\end{aligned}</math>
and
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
y &= -\mu^{1/2} \sqrt{2} \sin\theta + \mu \left(+\frac 43 \sin(2\theta)-\frac 13 \cos(2\theta)+1\right) \\
  &\qquad + \mu^{3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{72}} \left( - 5\sin(3\theta) + 7\cos(3\theta) + 36\sin\theta + 28\cos\theta \right) + \mathcal{O}(\mu^2)
\end{aligned}</math>

This provides a [[parametric equation]] for the limit cycle. This is plotted in the illustration on the right.

<gallery mode="nolines" widths="300" heights="300" caption="Examples of bifurcations">
File:Hopf_and_homoclinic_bifurcation.gif|A Hopf bifurcation occurs in the system <math>\frac{d x}{d t}=\mu x+y-x^2 </math> and <math> \frac{d y}{d t}=-x+\mu y+2 x^2 </math>, when <math>\mu = 0</math>, around the origin. A [[homoclinic bifurcation]] occurs around <math>\mu = 0.06605695</math>.
File:Hopf_and_homoclinic_bifurcation_2.gif|A detailed view of the homoclinic bifurcation.
